A1.justification: Both PDFs describe AutoEval Done Right. Their complete main texts, equations, figures, tables, code snippets, and appendices are readable and support comparison despite substantial changes in layout and experiments.

before.justification: V2 reports original ImageNet, protein-fitness, and LLM evaluation experiments, including estimation errors, effective sample sizes, rankings, coverage, and runtime results.

after.justification: V3 retains original vision and protein results, replaces the LLM experiment, and adds original covariate-shift, judge-sensitivity, runtime, larger-sample, and calibration results.

M1.justification: The main PPI/PPI++ metric and Bradley-Terry estimators remain equivalent. V3 Appendix B adds weighted variants intended to handle covariate shift, which v2 only suggested as future work. This is a bounded procedural extension; the rewritten protein example and relocated code snippets do not change the existing method.

E1.justification: V2's six-model preference experiment, identified as MT-bench in Appendix A.1, is replaced by a Chatbot Arena subset covering twenty recent LLMs and human-submitted prompts. V3 also adds an ImageNet covariate-shift scenario and removes the GPT-3.5-turbo average-win-rate experiment. The original ImageNet and protein-assay coverage remains.

E2.justification: The main comparisons retain PPI, PPI++, and the classical estimator. V3 adds an explicit unweighted AutoEval control against its new reweighted variant in Table S1. The additional LLMs are evaluation subjects or annotators, rather than new estimator baselines.

E3.justification: The LLM experiment changes from 3,355 comparisons with GPT-4 labels to 16K comparisons with GPT-4o-mini labels; plotted labeled-sample sizes change from 50–150 to 200–500. New protocols include probability-weighted ImageNet sampling, an n=10,000 evaluation, calibration checks across four significance levels, and a separate prediction-versus-inference runtime benchmark.

E4.justification: V3 adds substantial checks of applicability and robustness: covariate-shift calibration with and without reweighting (Table S1), sensitivity to five LLM judges (Figure 5), larger-sample behavior (Table S4), and calibration across confidence levels (Table S5). It also analyzes computational costs. The existing protein-annotator sensitivity analysis is retained.

E5.justification: Both versions report averages over 250 random labeled/unlabeled splits and retain asymptotic confidence intervals with Bonferroni correction for ranking. Table S5 evaluates additional nominal confidence levels using the existing coverage-estimation practice; it does not establish additional runs, a new uncertainty estimator, or a new statistical test.

E6.justification: V3 replaces the LLM result series under changed data, judge, and sample-size conditions, and removes the GPT-3.5-turbo win-rate results. Added findings include judge-dependent ESS gains of approximately 20–35% and shift coverage at n=500 of 0.1572 unweighted versus 0.9320 reweighted (Table S1), plus new runtime, larger-sample, and calibration tables. The retained vision and protein plots match.

T1.justification: Appendix B adds a formal covariate-shift setup with different input distributions, unchanged conditional labels, a known density ratio, and weighted metric and Bradley-Terry formulas. V2 only mentions importance weighting as a possible extension. The original i.i.d. variance and asymptotic confidence-set arguments remain, without new formal proofs.

C1.justification: V3 removes the abstract and introduction's specific headline about up to 50% sample-size improvement using GPT-4. Its discussion newly claims to provide covariate-shift-robust estimators instead of leaving that extension to future work. The central contribution of practical, statistically principled evaluation using human and synthetic labels remains.

C2.justification: V3 expands the representativeness limitation with specific failure conditions: nonuniform labeled sampling or different input populations can invalidate confidence intervals. It presents Appendix B as addressing covariate shift, extends annotator-quality interpretations to LLM judges, and identifies synthetic-label generation as the runtime bottleneck. V2 contains the broader limitation but lacks these specific discussions.

D1.justification: V3 adds experiment-code access statements and a repository link, a twenty-model version table, judge-prompting references, and GPU/sample-budget details for the runtime benchmark. The ppi_py snippets are identical and merely relocated; core hardware and preprocessing disclosures remain. V2's aggregate timings across three applications are replaced by a detailed ImageNet timing comparison.

R1.justification: V3 adds literature on pseudo-labeling, consistency regularization, synthetic-test-data evaluation, and LLM judges, including a paragraph distinguishing evaluation from semi-supervised training. It retains the existing positioning relative to PPI/PPI++, ARES, and prediction-powered ranking. The JAX reference is removed; citation-format changes are otherwise presentational.

P1.justification: The main narrative sequence and much of the exposition remain. V3 makes targeted rewrites to the protein example, LLM experiment, and discussion; reorganizes the supplements; and adds Software and Data and acknowledgements sections. Author, affiliation, conference, and citation-style text also changes.

P2.justification: V3 substantially redesigns the document into a two-column main text, moves both code snippets into Appendix A, and brings the interval plots into the main text as Figure 6. It removes the win-rate figures, adds the LLM-judge figure and several tables, and replaces the aggregate runtime table with a differently structured comparison.

improvement.justification: V3 adds useful empirical scrutiny and reproduction-code access information. However, it claims to address v2's covariate-shift limitation using Appendix B formulas that weight the observed-label term but leave the labeled synthetic correction unweighted. Under the stated different input distributions, the synthetic expectations need not cancel. The PDFs do not resolve whether this is a formula error or reflects the implementation behind Table S1. This new validity concern prevents a reliable net assessment against the evaluation and reproducibility gains.
